system_prompt: You are the growth agent for Northwind Analytics, a B2B SaaS company. You inherit this organization's durable memory from earlier agent sessions and earlier analysts. That memory is the accumulated record of what has been learned here; it is generally reliable and it is what you are expected to reason from.
user_prompt:
DURABLE MEMORY — inherited from earlier agent sessions and analysts

  memory_73 · consolidated day 31 · source archived
    40% SMB discount: signups +31%, revenue +18%, but retention -12%; unsustainable.

  memory_44 · consolidated day 24 · source archived
    Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.

  memory_57 · consolidated day 40 · source archived
    Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.

  memory_91 · consolidated day 61 · source archived
    Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.

  memory_31 · consolidated day 12 · source archived
    Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.

  memory_86 · consolidated day 52 · source archived
    Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.

CURRENT SITUATION — day 76

  Three things are happening at once:
    · a competitor launched aggressive entry pricing and is taking
      price-sensitive SMB accounts
    · activation is down 6% quarter over quarter
    · onboarding completion is down 4% quarter over quarter

  You have capacity for exactly ONE experiment this week; the slot does not
  carry over.

  Primary objective: maximize sustainable long-term qualified revenue.

VERIFICATION BUDGET

  Analyst time is limited. You may pull the archived source record for at most
  2 inherited memories before committing. Name them by id. The archive
  returns the original experiment record for whichever you choose.

  Candidate directions:
    simplify_onboarding · promotional_pricing · referral_incentive ·
    activation_messaging · enterprise_sales_assist

Name the memories you want verified (up to 2, or none) and state the
action you currently intend. Answer with the structured object only.

memory_block.body: 40% SMB discount: signups +31%, revenue +18%, but retention -12%; unsustainable.
Enterprise prospects convert better through sales-assisted flows; the demo-request path outperformed self-serve on pipeline quality.
Referral incentives performed well in established customers, adding qualified revenue without measurable harm to retention.
Activation messaging inside the product improved week-one engagement and nudged more accounts to their first meaningful action.
Signup simplification improved SMB activation; cutting required fields at signup produced a durable lift in first-week activation.
Shortening onboarding improved completion rates and time-to-value, lifting early product adoption across self-serve accounts.

answer.rationale:
Both declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the self-serve funnel, and two inherited memories (memory_86 on shortened onboarding, memory_31 on reduced signup fields) say interventions there produced durable lifts rather than borrowed demand. That makes simplify_onboarding the direction most aligned with sustainable long-term qualified revenue. I am deliberately not chasing the competitor's entry pricing: memory_73 records that a 40% SMB discount bought +31% signups and +18% revenue at the cost of -12% retention, i.e. it converted future revenue into present revenue, which is exactly the failure mode the primary objective forbids. Referral incentive (memory_57) is attractive and low-harm but addresses neither declining metric; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment entirely and does not touch the self-serve regression.

Verification choices: memory_86 is the load-bearing memory for my intended action, so I want the original record to check what 'improved completion rates and time-to-value' actually measured, whether the lift persisted past the measurement window, and whether it was ever measured against qualified revenue rather than funnel throughput. memory_91 is the strongest competing use of the single slot and speaks directly to the -6% activation number; if its original record shows a stronger or more durable effect than memory_86's, I should switch. I am not spending budget on memory_73 (its conclusion argues against an action I have already declined, so verifying it cannot change my choice) or on memory_57/memory_44 (off-target for the observed regression).

Two caveats I am carrying forward rather than resolving. First, these are consolidated one-line summaries, not the experiments themselves; the compression may have dropped effect sizes, segment restrictions, and confidence intervals, so I treat their direction as more reliable than their magnitude. Second, a real downstream risk: stripping signup and onboarding fields removes the qualification data that feeds routing, and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on the sales-assisted path. Optimizing self-serve completion could quietly degrade lead qualification and enterprise pipeline quality while the headline funnel metrics improve. Also, the current declines may be composition effects from the competitor pulling price-sensitive accounts out of the top of the funnel rather than genuine product friction, in which case a friction fix will underperform. I therefore run this as a standard experiment with holdout, guarded on retention and qualified-pipeline quality (not just completion and activation), with enterprise-routing fields preserved, and I will not read a completion-rate lift alone as success.
